2.title: A Nursing Mother and a Urging Father
2.overview: After Paul’s hurried departure, someone was evidently calling him just another travelling religious salesman who ran when it got hard. Paul answers by appealing to what the Thessalonians saw with their own eyes, from his arrival bruised from Philippi to his nights at a workbench. He thanks God that they received his message as God’s word, though it cost them persecution. Then his grief shows: he was “orphaned” from them, Satan blocked his return, yet they are his hope, joy and crown when the Lord Jesus comes.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reminds them how the mission began: bold preaching after Philippi, no flattery or greed, a mother’s gentleness, a man paying his own way, and a father’s urging to live worthily of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The minister as steward, not owner

The governing idea of the passage is in verse 4: entrusted with the gospel. A minister stands under the word, not over it; he is a steward, never an entrepreneur. And the God who approved him goes on testing his heart, so the question in every sermon and conversation is whose verdict he is working for.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The circuit Paul travelled was worked by professional lecturers who lived on their rhetoric. So Paul answers with what could be checked: they had watched him arrive injured and preach anyway, and watched him at a leatherworker’s bench before dawn and after dark.

Now: For anyone holding office, the question is almost never whether you have a right, but what you intend to do with it.

verseByVerse.quote: For you yourselves know, brothers, that our coming to you was not in vain. But though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi, as you know, we had boldness in our God to declare to you the gospel of God in the midst of much conflict.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Thessalonians 2 is Paul’s defence of his ministry in Thessalonica. After his sudden departure, opponents seem to have said he was another travelling preacher, in it for money or fame, who abandoned his converts at the first sign of trouble. Paul reminds them what they saw: boldness despite suffering, no flattery or greed, a nursing mother’s gentleness, work night and day, and a father’s exhortation (vv. 1–12). He thanks God that they received his message as the word of God and endured persecution as the Judean churches had (vv. 13–16). His absence was not his choice, and they are his crown at Christ’s coming (vv. 17–20). Behind this portrait of a true pastor stands, at every turn, the Chief Shepherd whose likeness Paul bears.

The accusation behind the chapter. You can hear the accusation’s shape in what Paul denies: that he was a flatterer, after money, chasing a reputation, and that he ran when it got difficult. Travelling philosophers and religious salesmen worked that circuit constantly, and the easiest way to damage a young church was to persuade it that its founder had been another of them. So Paul keeps saying, you know: you were there. His defence is their own memory.

Not in vain. The word is kenos, empty, hollow. The congregation reading the letter was the proof that it was not.

Shamefully treated at Philippi. In Philippi he and Silas had been stripped in the marketplace, beaten with rods and fastened in the stocks (Acts 16:22–24), illegally, since they were Roman citizens. He arrived in Thessalonica, a hundred miles on, still marked.

Boldness in our God. He preached anyway. The verb (parrēsiazomai) is the freedom to speak openly, and its source is in our God, not his own nerve: borrowed courage, the opposite of the boast he is accused of.

In the midst of much conflict. The word is agōn, the struggle in the arena, and it ended in a riot (Acts 17:5).

The cost is the credential. The chapter’s argument in miniature: a man in it for money or applause does not walk from a flogging in one city into a riot in the next.

Shamefully treated, like his Lord. The word Paul uses for Philippi (hybrizō) is the word Jesus used of his own coming suffering: the Son of Man would be delivered over to the Gentiles and mocked and shamefully treated and spat upon (Luke 18:32). Paul was walking where his Lord had walked first (Acts 5:41). A man who preaches a Christ who was insulted and beaten does not find insult a reason to stop; he finds it a strange confirmation that he belongs to the one he preaches.

Where does boldness come from, if I am naturally timid? From God, not from temperament. Paul did not say he was brave; he said he had boldness in our God. Courage of this kind grows from being sure of the message, sure of the God who sends it, and more concerned for the hearer than for yourself. Pray for it, as the apostles did (Acts 4:29). Then take the next small step: one honest sentence about Christ to one person. Boldness is usually given in the act of obeying, not beforehand.

Should I keep speaking about Christ after I have been hurt for it? Usually yes, though wisdom matters. Paul moved on from Philippi but did not go silent; he preached in the next city. Sometimes the right thing is to leave a hostile place, as he did more than once. But being hurt is not a sign God has withdrawn his call. Bring the wound to him, let others in the church care for you, and then speak again when he opens the door.
verseByVerse.note: At Philippi Paul and Silas had been beaten and jailed just before they came to Thessalonica.

verseByVerse.quote: For our appeal does not spring from error or impurity or any attempt to deceive, but just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, so we speak, not to please man, but to please God who tests our hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Error, impurity, deceit. The three denials cover three ways a ministry goes wrong. Error (planē) is about the message: a man may be sincere and simply wrong. Impurity (akatharsia) is about motive, and the word often carried a sexual edge; a travelling teacher with access to households was a known hazard. Deceit (dolos) is about method: cunning trickery, the angler’s art of hiding the hook. Any one of them is enough to ruin a ministry that is sound in the other two.

Approved by God. Approved (dokimazō) is the assayer’s word for testing metal and finding it genuine. Paul did not appoint himself: God tested him, found him fit and gave him the gospel to carry (1 Timothy 1:12), and goes on examining his heart every time he speaks.

Entrusted. Like a steward with his master’s goods (1 Corinthians 4:1–2), Paul is a courier carrying something that belongs to someone else, and a courier does not get to edit the parcel.

To please God who tests our hearts. Everything turns on this sentence (Galatians 1:10). It is not indifference to people, as the tenderness that follows shows, but a question of which verdict he works for. The two audiences pull constantly in opposite directions: one can be pleased by softening what is hard, and the other sees the heart while you do it.

The one who always pleased the Father. Jesus said of the Father, I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29), and Paul says of him that Christ did not please himself (Romans 15:3). He slipped away from the crowd that wanted to make him king by force (John 6:15), and he refused the devil’s offer of the kingdoms without a cross (Matthew 4:8–10). Every faithful courier of the gospel is copying that one life, and every one of them falls short of it.

What does it look like to please people rather than God? It looks like leaving out the parts of the truth that would cost you: never mentioning repentance or judgement, agreeing with whoever is in the room, staying silent when a friend is going wrong, shaping what you say by what will be liked. It is often driven by fear dressed up as kindness. Pleasing God does not mean being harsh; Paul was gentle. It means saying the true thing in a loving way, and letting God judge the result.

For worship. The gospel is God’s treasure, not ours, and he has been pleased to put it into clay jars, carrying a light that is not their own (2 Corinthians 4:7). The God who tests hearts found in his Son a heart that passed every test, and he has made that Son our righteousness, so that tried and failing servants stand approved in him.

verseByVerse.quote: For we never came with words of flattery, as you know, nor with a pretext for greed—God is witness. Nor did we seek glory from people, whether from you or from others, though we could have made demands as apostles of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Words of flattery. Flattery is saying what a person wants to hear in order to get something from them: praise with a hook in it. For this charge Paul appeals to their memory: you heard what I actually said.

A pretext for greed. A pretext (prophasis) is a cover story: ministry as a front for making money. But greed is a motive, and motives are invisible, so Paul calls the one witness who can see them.

Glory from people. This is subtler than money and more common among religious people: a man can be scrupulous about cash and still feed on being admired. And not from you or from others means he was not building a reputation to spend somewhere else.

We could have made demands. Literally, though we could have been a weight: they could have stood on their dignity and asked for support. Paul defends that right elsewhere (1 Corinthians 9:4–14), and declines to press it.

The mind of Christ. This is the mind of Christ, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped (Philippians 2:6). The question in ministry, as in every relationship where one person holds power, is almost never whether you have a right. Usually you do. It is what you intend to do with the right you have.

How can I tell encouragement from flattery in myself? Ask three questions. Is it true? Flattery exaggerates or invents. Is it for their good or for mine? Flattery wants something back: favour, a contract, to be liked. Would I say it behind their back too? Flattery is spoken to the face only. Encouragement names real grace in someone, specifically, and then gives God the credit. Practise that kind freely; the church is starved of it.

Is it wrong to want to be appreciated? No. Paul longed to be loved by his churches, and it is human to be glad when your work is valued. What is wrong is making people’s praise the reason you serve, so that you sulk when it is missing or shape the work to get it. Do the work for God, receive thanks gratefully when it comes, and pass the glory on.

verseByVerse.quote: But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother taking care of her own children. So, being affectionately desirous of you, we were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you had become very dear to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we were gentle among you. Having said what he was not, Paul says what he was. Gentle (ēpioi) is the opposite of domineering. Paul, the man of iron in Galatians, is soft with these new believers.

The textual question. The Greek manuscripts divide between ēpioi, gentle, and nēpioi, infants, one letter apart, as the ESV footnote notes. Several of the earliest read infants, and some modern Bibles (the NIV) follow them. If it is infants, Paul says he became like a small child among them, without airs or demands, before shifting to the nursing mother. Either reading tells against the charge of self-importance, and the ESV’s gentle gives the smoother sense.

Like a nursing mother. The phrase her own is doing real work: not a hired wet nurse minding somebody else’s baby, but a mother feeding her own child. The verb (thalpō) means to cherish, to keep warm, and is used of a bird brooding over her eggs: the most ordinary and costly self-giving, at night, unseen.

Affectionately desirous. The word homeiromai appears nowhere else in the New Testament and is known elsewhere chiefly from a gravestone where grieving parents use it, it seems, of a lost child: the ache of wanting someone you cannot reach. That is what Paul felt for a church he had known for a month or so.

Our own selves. The word for selves (psychai) means lives: time, energy, hearts. It is possible to deliver the message accurately and withhold the man, and much religious professionalism is exactly that: correct content, carefully rationed distance. Gospel ministry is life on life.

Very dear to us. That is the reason, and it is not a strategy. Love hands over more than was required, and anyone served by someone who plainly liked them knows the difference.

More than his life shared. Paul’s self-giving copies something far larger. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), the same word for life that Paul uses here. But Paul offered his time, strength and heart; Christ, in Paul’s own words, loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20), and at his table he says, this is my body, given for you (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24). The messenger is the message, and he gave himself with it.

Is it right for a male apostle to call himself a nursing mother? Yes, and it is beautiful. Scripture uses mother imagery for God’s own tenderness (Isaiah 49:15; 66:13), and Jesus longed to gather Jerusalem as a hen gathers her chicks (Matthew 23:37). Paul uses it to show the tenderness every true shepherd needs, not to blur the callings of men and women. Leaders in the church, who are to be qualified men, are not meant to be cold. (This commentary reads 1 Timothy 2:12 and 3:1–7 as giving the office of elder to qualified men; many faithful Christians read those passages differently, and the point here does not depend on it: no shepherd, of any view, is meant to be cold.) Their authority is the self-giving care of a mother at night as well as the steady formation of a father.

I am not a pastor. How do I share my life as well as the gospel? Open your ordinary life to people. Invite someone into your home, not just to an event. Let them see you pray, fail, apologise and keep trusting. Spend time with a younger believer, a lonely neighbour or a new member over months, not minutes. Share meals, lifts, worries. Most people are not won or grown by programmes but by being loved by a Christian who lets them close enough to see Christ at work.

For worship. Before Paul was a nursing mother to Thessalonica, God was one to Israel: can a woman forget her nursing child? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you, says the LORD (Isaiah 49:15). He has kept that word in his Son. The God who would not forget his children came and fed them with himself, the living bread given for the life of the world (John 6:51).

verseByVerse.quote: For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil: we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you, while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Labour and toil. The hardest evidence in the chapter. Kopos is labour to the point of exhaustion; mochthos is hardship, the grind. Paul is describing being tired.

We worked night and day. The trade was probably the tentmaking or leatherworking Luke mentions in Corinth (Acts 18:3; 20:34): heavy work gentlemen despised, at the bench before dawn and after dark, with the preaching fitted around it. Philippi also sent him gifts while he was in Thessalonica (Philippians 4:16), and even with that help he worked.

Not a weight on anyone. He could have made demands as an apostle (v. 6); instead he paid his own way, so that he would not burden a poor young church or give any ground to the charge of greed.

The answer without argument. A man running a religious racket does not work a double shift to avoid taking money from his converts. The Thessalonians would have seen him come to the meeting with his hands still rough from the workshop.

Free of charge. The work served the word. Paul’s hands earned bread so that his mouth could give away the bread of life without a price attached. The reason runs to the heart of the message. The gospel is free because it has been paid for. Christ, though he was rich, became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). A preacher who sold that news would misrepresent it, and a preacher who worked a double shift to give it away was preaching it with his hands.

Should my church pay its pastor, then? Yes, normally. Scripture says the labourer deserves his wages and that those who preach the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Timothy 5:17–18; 1 Corinthians 9:14). A paid pastor is not less spiritual than a self-supporting one. Paul’s choice in Thessalonica was a freedom he used for a reason, not a rule for every church. Churches should support their ministers generously, and ministers should guard their hearts against loving money.

Does ordinary work matter to God? Very much. Paul did not see the workshop as a distraction from real ministry. It was part of his witness. Your job, done honestly and well, is service to Christ (Colossians 3:23–24), provides for your family and the needy (4:11–12; Ephesians 4:28), and gives you daily contact with people who need the gospel. You do not have to leave work to serve God. You serve him there.
verseByVerse.note: Paul supported himself by his trade — he was a tentmaker.

verseByVerse.quote: You are witnesses, and God also, how holy and righteous and blameless was our conduct toward you believers. For you know how, like a father with his children, we exhorted each one of you and encouraged you and charged you to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into his own kingdom and glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are witnesses, and God also. Both courts again. Holy is devoted to God, righteous is just toward people, blameless is with nothing anyone could lay a charge on. Paul is not claiming sinlessness, but that no accusation would stick, which is testable. And he lived knowing that God watched the workshop and the private house as closely as the synagogue: God sees the hours no one else sees.

Like a father. The nursing mother (v. 7) carried warmth and self-giving; the father in the ancient household carried formation, responsibility for teaching and training, for what the child became.

Exhorted, encouraged, charged. Exhorted (parakaleō): coming alongside to urge. Encouraged (paramytheomai): putting heart into someone. Charged (martyromai): a solemn testifying that puts someone under obligation. A father who only encourages raises children who cannot stand; one who only charges raises children who leave.

Each one of you. In perhaps a month, while also working night and day at a bench, Paul dealt with these people individually, as he later did house to house in Ephesus (Acts 20:20). He knew them one at a time.

To walk in a manner worthy of God. Worthy is not a standard they must reach to earn something. It is a matching: conduct that fits who God is and what has happened to you, as a uniform fits the service you are in.

Who calls you into his own kingdom and glory. The calling is present and ongoing, toward the kingdom and glory that are their destination. That is Paul’s whole method of motivating people: not behave, or else, but this is where you are going; live like someone going there.

The glory is Christ’s. What is the glory God calls them into? Paul answers in his second letter: they were called through the gospel to obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Thessalonians 2:14), and those he called he also glorified, conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:29–30). So the walk worthy of God has a face: whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked (1 John 2:6).

What is God’s kingdom and glory, and am I in it now? God’s kingdom is his saving rule through Christ. It has already begun: believers have been transferred into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13). But its full glory is still to come when Christ returns, and that glory is a share in God’s own splendour, the life of the age to come in his presence (Romans 8:18; 2 Thessalonians 2:14). So you are in it now, and you are being called further into it. You are a citizen already, walking toward the capital.

What does living worthy of God look like on an ordinary day? It looks like the life Paul describes in chapters 4 and 5: sexual purity, brotherly love, quiet honest work, hope at the graveside, alertness, respect for leaders, patience with the weak, joy, prayer and thanksgiving. It is not a special religious mood but ordinary life brought under the King. When you are unsure what to do, ask what fits a child of God who is on the way to his glory.

verseByVerse.ref: 2:13–16 – How They Received the Word — and What It Cost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God that they received the message as what it truly is, God’s word, now at work in them. They have suffered from their own people as the churches in Judea did, and Paul speaks severely of those who killed the Lord and were trying to stop the gospel reaching the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.theology:
Scripture as God’s own speech

Verse 13 is one of the clearest statements in the New Testament of what Scripture is. Its authority does not wait on our verdict; but only those who hear it as God’s word find it working in them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verses 15–16 have been misused across the centuries. Paul, himself a Jew, names a target by its actions, in the insider language of covenant rebuke.

Now: The wrath of verse 16 must be read beside 1:10, where wrath is what Jesus delivers people from, Paul himself included. A sober warning is never a licence for contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: And we also thank God constantly for this, that when you received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God, which is at work in you believers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. Verses 1 to 12 defended the messengers; verse 13 turns to the message, thanking God a second time. If Paul had been a fraud, his word would be suspect too; but they had heard God in it, and verses 14–16 give the proof: the clearest proof that the word was at work is that they kept believing when it cost them their neighbours.

Received and accepted. They received it (paralambanō), the ordinary term for taking delivery of something; then they accepted it (dechomai), the word for welcoming a guest into your house. The first is hearing; the second is embracing. Plenty of people do the first every Sunday and never do the second.

What it really is. They heard it from a leatherworker with marks on his back, in a city full of competing lecturers. Nothing about the delivery compelled the verdict, yet they concluded they were being addressed by God, and Paul says they were right: what it really is.

The decision every hearer makes. Every hearer makes it, usually without noticing. If the Bible is a valuable human document, you weigh it, keep what persuades you, and remain the judge. If it is the word of God, the relation reverses and it reads you. There is no third option where it is God’s word and you still hold the editorial pencil.

At work in you. The verb is energeō, the root of our word energy, and it is present and continuous: the word is working in them now, while Paul writes (Hebrews 4:12; Isaiah 55:11).

Hearing the Lord in his messengers. Jesus had told his apostles that this would happen: the one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me (Luke 10:16). The Thessalonians heard a leatherworker and met the risen Christ, because the apostolic word is the word of Christ (Colossians 3:16), and his sheep hear their shepherd’s voice in it (John 10:27). You are not admiring Paul’s argument; you are being addressed by the Lord himself, and answering him.

Where Christians differ: is Scripture the word of God? Some say the Bible contains or becomes the word of God, or is merely human testimony. This commentary’s view: The apostles’ message, now written in Scripture, is what it really is: the word of God, not merely the words of men, though spoken through men. Scripture is God-breathed and authoritative in all it affirms (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21), as the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession confess (Westminster 1.4; 1689 1.4). Its authority does not depend on human acceptance; it is God’s word whether received or not, and it works in those who believe.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every preacher’s words are God’s word. Only as preaching faithfully conveys Scripture does it carry God’s authority.

How can a book written by men be God’s word? Because God spoke through them, not around them. He used their personalities, languages, research and circumstances, and so superintended their writing that what they wrote is exactly what he intended to say (2 Peter 1:21). Paul wrote as Paul, with his own warmth and style, and yet the Thessalonians were right to hear God. The human and divine are not rivals in Scripture any more than in the person of Christ, who is fully human and fully God.

Is it not circular to believe the Bible is God’s word because the Bible says so? Every final authority has to vouch for itself, or it would not be final. A person who trusts reason alone can only defend reason by reasoning. The Thessalonians were not argued into faith by a clever proof. They heard the word, and it did what only God’s word does: it showed them their idols, set Christ before them, and changed them. The Spirit himself convinces people that Scripture is God’s word as they hear it (Westminster 1.5; 1689 1.5), and he does it through its message, not apart from it. There are good reasons too: the resurrection of Jesus, and Jesus’ own trust in the Scriptures (John 10:35). But in the end God’s word is believed the way the sun is seen: by its own light. That cannot be proved like a sum, and an honest doubter is not a fool for asking; the invitation is the one the Thessalonians accepted, to hear it and see what it does.

How do I receive the word as God’s word when I read it? Come expecting God to speak, not merely to gather information. Pray before you read, asking him to open your eyes. Read to obey, not just to understand: ask what it shows you of God and Christ, what it promises, what it commands, and what you must believe or change. When it contradicts you, let it win. And keep coming back. The word works over time, like seed, not usually like lightning.

What about new revelations or prophecies today? The word that works in believers is the apostolic word, now complete in Scripture. The canon is closed: God has spoken finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and the apostles’ teaching is the foundation the church is built on (Ephesians 2:20). Impressions and promptings must always be tested by Scripture and never placed beside it. Everything we need for life and godliness is already given there.

verseByVerse.quote: For you, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God in Christ Jesus that are in Judea. For you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Imitators of the churches in Judea. Here they imitate congregations nearly a thousand miles away that they had never met, by enduring persecution as the first churches had.

Your own countrymen. The Judean believers were opposed by fellow Jews (Acts 8:1–3; 12:1–3); the Thessalonian believers by fellow Thessalonians, stirred up by some of the synagogue (Acts 17:5–9). In each case it came from the neighbours, which costs most.

What that meant in that city. These Gentiles had walked out of the guild dinners, household shrines and civic festivals, and the pressure came from employers, families and old friends.

Joining a line. A young church under attack asks in the night whether something has gone wrong. Paul’s answer: they have joined a line with the oldest churches. Their suffering is not evidence that they took a wrong turn. It is evidence that they are on the road.

The road their Lord walked first. The line goes back further: their suffering was Christ’s before it was theirs. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11); even his brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5). And he told his disciples to expect the same: if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (John 15:20). The Thessalonians were walking in his footprints, and those footprints lead through a cross to an empty tomb.

What it does not mean. It does not mean persecution proves a church true. Plenty of people are disliked for being disagreeable. But faithful churches should expect it (2 Timothy 3:12), and opposition is not proof of failure either, which is what the frightened heart assumes at three in the morning.

My own family opposes my faith. What should I do? You are in good company: Jesus said a person’s enemies may be those of his own household (Matthew 10:36), and the Thessalonians suffered from their own people. Stay loving, respectful and patient. Honour your parents and serve your family in every way that does not require disobeying Christ. Do not argue constantly; let your life speak, and speak when asked. Keep bringing them to God in prayer. Find support in your church family. And where there is any threat of harm, seek help and safety; enduring hostility is not the same as tolerating abuse.

Why does it help to know others suffer the same? Because suffering isolates and lies. It says you are alone, and that it means God has abandoned you. Knowing that Christians across the world and down the centuries have walked this road answers both lies. You belong to a family that has always suffered and always been kept. That is why it is right to pray for and learn about the persecuted church today: they strengthen us, and we can strengthen them.

For worship. When Saul of Tarsus was dragging believers out of their houses, the risen Lord stopped him on the road and asked, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). The Head feels every blow that lands on his body. No believer pushed out of a guild or a family suffers out of his sight; and the voice that asked that question turned the persecutor into a brother.

verseByVerse.quote: who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and drove us out, and displease God and oppose all mankind by hindering us from speaking to the Gentiles that they might be saved—so as always to fill up the measure of their sins. But wrath has come upon them at last!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hardest passage in the letter. This passage has been misused across the centuries to justify appalling things, so it must be read carefully and its limits stated plainly.

Who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets. Paul is himself a Jew, a Hebrew of Hebrews (Philippians 3:5), who insists in Romans that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1). Whatever this passage means, it cannot mean what Romans denies. Nor is he condemning a race. His target is specific and he names their actions: the leaders who rejected Christ and handed him over, following a long pattern of killing the prophets (Matthew 23:29–37; Acts 7:52).

The language of covenant rebuke. The charge sheet is drawn from Israel’s own Scriptures. The prophets said harder things about their nation’s leaders than Paul does here, and Jesus lamented over Jerusalem as the city that kills the prophets (Matthew 23:37). This is the internal language of covenant rebuke, spoken by an insider, which it stops being when outsiders pick it up as a weapon.

And drove us out. From Thessalonica and then from Beroea (Acts 17:5–10, 13). This had happened a few months earlier.

Oppose all mankind. It sounds sweeping, but it is aimed at one thing: obstructing the gospel from going to the nations, which is to act against humanity as such. It is a charge about the mission, not about race.

Fill up the measure. As God waited until the sin of the Amorites was complete (Genesis 15:16), and as Jesus told the leaders of his day to fill up the measure of their fathers (Matthew 23:32), so these opponents were filling up their sins to the point of judgement. God’s patience is long, and it has an end.

Wrath has come. The verb is past: already come. Judgement is so certain that it can be spoken of as arrived, the prophetic past tense; within twenty years Jerusalem and the temple would fall (AD 70). At last may also mean fully, or to the end.

Did Paul write these verses? Some scholars think vv. 13–16 were added by a later writer, because they sound so harsh and seem to look back on the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. But no manuscript lacks them, and they fit Paul’s own experience of being driven out by Jewish opponents (Acts 17:5, 13). Nor are they a verdict on the Jewish people: Paul himself was a Jew who longed for their salvation (Romans 9:1–3; 10:1).

Where Christians differ: is this anti-Jewish? Some say this passage is anti-Semitic, or that it was not written by Paul. This commentary’s view: Paul, himself a Jew, is speaking of those who opposed the gospel, not of the Jewish people as a whole. He loved his people deeply and longed for their salvation (Romans 9:1–5; 10:1), and many of the first believers were Jews. His language echoes Jesus and the prophets, who spoke similarly to Israel. Christians must never use this passage to justify hatred of Jews, which is a terrible sin that has stained church history.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all Jews are under wrath, or that Jews alone killed Jesus. Gentiles shared in it (Acts 4:27), and our sins put him there.

The passage ends where the letter began. Wrath is what Jesus delivers people from (1:10), including Paul, once a persecutor hindering the gospel, and rescued. Opposition to the gospel places any people, Jew or Gentile, under the wrath the gospel exists to save them from, and the same gospel stands open to them. The opponents were not irreligious men but zealous ones, as Paul had been (Galatians 1:13–14). Religion used to earn a standing with God can make a person the fiercest enemy of grace, because grace tells him his record counts for nothing. A sober warning is not a licence for contempt, and anyone who has used this passage for contempt has read the man who wrote Romans 11 exactly backwards.

Does this passage settle what God will do with Israel in the future? No. It describes the judgement on those who were rejecting Christ and blocking the gospel in Paul’s own day. Whether Romans 11 promises a large-scale turning of the Jewish people to Christ before the end is a question on which faithful Reformed Christians differ, and this verse does not decide it. What every view agrees on is that Jewish people, like everyone, are saved only through faith in Jesus the Messiah, and that the church should long and pray for their salvation, as Paul did.

How should I treat people who oppose the gospel? Pray for them, love them, and keep telling them the truth. Paul could describe his opponents in the strongest terms and still spend his life preaching to them. Remember that you yourself were once an enemy of God (Romans 5:10), and that the fiercest opponent of the church in that generation became its greatest missionary. Leave judgement to God, and never return hatred for hatred.

For worship. The Lord Jesus was killed by the hands of lawless men, Jew and Gentile together, and our sins were in their hands. And from the cross he prayed, Father, forgive them (Luke 23:34, a prayer missing from some early manuscripts but widely received as genuine). The wrath opposition to God deserves fell on him, so that persecutors like Saul could be made apostles, and enemies like us sons.
verseByVerse.note: Paul, himself a Jew, is speaking of those who opposed the gospel, as he had once done — not of every Jewish person.

parallels.desc: the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete

verseByVerse.ref: 2:17–20 – Orphaned From Them, and What He Expects to Hold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Torn away from them, Paul tried more than once to return, but Satan blocked the way. They are his hope, joy and crown at the Lord’s coming.
verseByVerse.theology:
The coming, and the pastor’s wreath

The reward of pastoral work is not the admiration of the present age but the sight, on that day, of people standing before Jesus because the gospel was faithfully preached and patiently tended.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The enemy who blocked Paul’s road did not win: Timothy went in his place, and this letter exists because Paul could not come.

Now: On the last day, is what you expect to hold up a record of what you achieved, or people who are standing there because of it?

verseByVerse.quote: But since we were torn away from you, brothers, for a short time, in person not in heart, we endeavored the more eagerly and with great desire to see you face to face, because we wanted to come to you—I, Paul, again and again—but Satan hindered us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Torn away. Torn away is aporphanisthentes, built on the word for orphan. Having called himself their mother and father, Paul is now the bereaved one. And his departure was forced (Acts 17:10); he did not abandon them, as his critics said.

In person not in heart. Two qualifications keep the grief from despair: the separation is temporary, and only physical.

The more eagerly. Opponents said he did not care; being torn away made him try harder.

I, Paul, again and again. He interrupts his own plural to sign his name: he tried, personally and repeatedly.

Satan hindered us. The verb (enkoptō) means to block or hinder, as by breaking up a road. Paul does not give the mechanism: it may have been the bond the authorities took from Jason (Acts 17:9), which made his return dangerous for his hosts, or illness, or hostility elsewhere. He read it as the work of an enemy keeping a young church from its teacher.

Can Satan thwart God’s plans? He can hinder our plans, but only within God’s permission, as with Job (Job 1–2) and Paul’s thorn (2 Corinthians 12:7). Paul was kept from Thessalonica, and God used even that: this letter was written because he could not come. God’s purposes are never defeated.

Where Christians differ: Satan’s power over circumstances. Some blame Satan for every difficulty; others ignore him. This commentary’s view: Satan is real and does oppose God’s work, sometimes through circumstances (Job 1–2; 2 Corinthians 12:7). But he acts only within the limits God permits, and God overrules even his opposition for good (Romans 8:28). Elsewhere Luke tells us the Spirit prevented Paul from going somewhere (Acts 16:6–7). Discernment is needed, and in every case we trust God’s sovereign providence, as the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach (Westminster 5.4; 1689 5.4).

Hold it with care, in both directions. Not every delay is a demonic assault, but Paul did not think his frustrations merely administrative. And he never says Satan won. Timothy went instead (3:2), and the letter you are reading was written because Paul could not come, which is not a bad accounting of who was hindered in the end.

Not left as orphans. The orphan word recalls a promise. On the night before he died, Jesus told his disciples, I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you (John 14:18), and he spoke of the Spirit who would be with them for ever. The apostle could be kept away; the Lord could not, for he was present among them by his Spirit.

How can I tell whether Satan is hindering me or God is closing a door? Often you cannot tell, and you do not need to. Paul read one blocked road as Satan’s work and another as the Spirit’s, and in both he did the same thing: trusted God, kept praying, and did what he could do. Ask whether the plan was clearly good and in line with Scripture. Keep seeking it by lawful means. If the door stays shut, accept it from God’s hand, and look for the other way he may be opening, as Timothy went when Paul could not.

Is it right to grieve over separation from Christian friends? Yes. Paul felt it like bereavement and was not ashamed to say so. Love for brothers and sisters in Christ is meant to be strong enough to hurt when we are parted. Bring the ache to God, keep in touch as you can (Paul wrote a letter and sent a friend), and remember that every separation between believers is for a short time. There is a day of reunion that no road-block can stop.

verseByVerse.quote: For what is our hope or joy or crown of boasting before our Lord Jesus at his coming? Is it not you? For you are our glory and joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what is our hope or joy or crown of boasting before our Lord Jesus at his coming? Paul has been defending himself against the charge of chasing glory (v. 6). Now, at the end of the chapter, he says what he is actually after, and the answer is the people he is writing to. He asks it as a question and answers it himself, and the effect is warmer than a statement would have been.

Crown. The stephanos is the victor’s wreath, also presented when a king or emperor visited.

At his coming. The word is parousia, in ordinary Greek the state visit of a sovereign to one of his cities, when the citizens streamed out to meet him on the road and escorted him in.

Is it not you? So the picture is this: the King arrives, and Paul is standing there, and what he has to show is not a record of his labours but a group of people. Their being there is the wreath.

The accusation settled. Paul’s glory and joy are them, now as then (Philippians 4:1), and that settles the accusation better than any denial. A man seeking glory from people uses them and moves on. Paul’s glory is them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s salvation depended on them. His hope of eternal life rested on Christ alone. It means they will be the joy and fruit of his labour.

Will Christians receive rewards in heaven? Yes. Scripture speaks of crowns and rewards given by Christ (1 Corinthians 3:12–14; 2 Timothy 4:8), not to earn salvation, which is a free gift, but as the Father’s gracious recognition of what his children did by his grace. Even our rewards are gifts: God crowns his own works in us. And the greatest reward is not a thing but a joy: to see Christ, and to see with him the people we loved and served for his sake.

Will we recognise one another when Christ comes? Paul expects to: he looks forward to standing with these very people before the Lord. Scripture never suggests we lose who we are in glory. The disciples recognised Moses and Elijah, and the risen Jesus was known by his friends. Paul will build on this in chapter 4, where the dead and the living are brought together to meet the Lord. Christian love is not ended by death; it is gathered up into the joy of his coming.

For worship. The King is coming, and his people will go out to meet him. On that day every faithful labour will be seen for what it was. For Christ, too, has a joy set before him: the people his Father gave him, brought home. Glory to the coming King.

3.title: Standing Firm in the Lord
3.overview: Paul could not bear not knowing whether the young church had survived persecution, so he sent Timothy back to strengthen them. Now Timothy has returned with good news: their faith and love are holding. Paul says, “now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord,” and the chapter ends in a prayer that looks ahead to the rest of the letter: love that overflows, and hearts blameless in holiness when Jesus comes.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:1–5 – Timothy Sent, and Suffering as a Posting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy to strengthen them, so that no one would be shaken by the suffering he had warned them to expect, and for fear that the tempter had undone his work.
verseByVerse.theology:
Affliction as appointment, not accident

Suffering for the gospel is a placement, not an accident. God governs all things, his people’s afflictions included, and he makes such suffering purposeful, producing endurance, character and hope (Romans 5:3–4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul feared not that persecution would smash this church but that it would coax them out of it (v. 3).

Now: Honest preparation for hardship is a form of pastoral care, and leaving it out is no kindness (v. 4).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone, and we sent Timothy, our brother and God's coworker in the gospel of Christ, to establish and exhort you in your faith,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Thessalonians 3 shows a pastor’s heart in anxiety and relief. Paul sends Timothy from Athens to steady them (vv. 1–5), comes alive again at his good news (vv. 6–10), and prays for a road back, overflowing love and hearts blameless at Christ’s coming (vv. 11–13). Behind the human drama stands the God who keeps his people when their pastor cannot reach them.

Could bear it no longer. The verb is stegō, to hold in, as a roof keeps out rain. Paul says it twice in five verses (vv. 1, 5): a man telling you what the months had been like.

Left behind at Athens alone. Athens, where he was mocked for mentioning resurrection and made few converts (Acts 17:15–34), was some of the thinnest ground he ever worked, and there he gave away his companion. Paul, whose letters are full of names, chose isolation because a frightened congregation needed someone more than he did: sharing not only the gospel but his own self (2:8), at an actual price.

God’s coworker. God’s coworker is a startling title for a young man. Some manuscripts read God’s servant, as the ESV notes, probably because copyists found the bolder title surprising.

To establish and exhort. To establish (stērizō) is to make firm, as you might prop up a leaning wall; to exhort (parakaleō) is to come alongside and urge. Both are about stability rather than growth: when a church is under attack, the first task is to keep it standing.

The Lord who establishes. Timothy was sent to do what, in the end, only the Lord can do. Paul prays that God would establish their hearts (3:13), and writes in his second letter that the Lord is faithful; he will establish you and guard you against the evil one (2 Thessalonians 3:3). Timothy was the means; the one holding up the leaning wall was the risen Christ, who said, I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18). Timothy worked on a building whose Builder never leaves the site.

If God keeps his people, why was Paul so anxious? Because God keeps his people through means, and Paul was one of the means. Trusting God’s sovereignty never made Paul passive; it made him pray and send. His anxiety was the anxiety of love, not of unbelief, and he did with it what love should do: he acted, and he brought it to God. Your concern for a struggling believer is not a lack of faith. It may be God’s way of moving you to be the help he intends.

What does following up a new believer actually involve? What Timothy did: going to them, strengthening their grasp of the truth, encouraging them to keep going, and preparing them for trouble. In practice that means meeting regularly, reading the Bible together, answering questions, praying with them, introducing them to other believers, and noticing when they go quiet. It does not require a title. It requires time, patience and love, and it is some of the most fruitful work in the church.

For worship. Paul chose to be alone in Athens so that a frightened church would not be alone. Long before, the Son of God let every friend leave him so that his people would never be left: you will leave me alone, he told them, yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me (John 16:32). Because he was deserted, not one of his own is ever abandoned. And he lets ordinary believers share the work as his coworkers.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one be moved by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that we are destined for this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That no one be moved. The verb is sainō, first used of a dog wagging its tail, so to fawn or coax, and later to unsettle. Paul’s worry is not only that persecution would smash them, but that they might be gently coaxed back to the life they had left.

How faith is usually lost. Not in a moment of dramatic renunciation, but by erosion: the family who keep asking, the invitation it is easier to accept, the guild dinner it costs too much to refuse. A wagging tail, not a battering ram.

Destined for this. The verb is keimetha: we are laid, set in place, as Paul was set in prison for the defence of the gospel (Philippians 1:16). Affliction did not slip past God’s attention; it is a placement (John 16:33; 2 Timothy 3:12).

The pastoral logic. What steadies a shaken believer is not being told the trouble will stop, but being told it is not a mistake. If suffering means the plan has gone wrong, every hard week is evidence against the faith; if suffering is where God has laid you, the hard week proves only that you are where he put you.

Appointed first for Christ. The placement began with Christ. On the road to Emmaus the risen Lord asked, was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? (Luke 24:26). His suffering was not an accident God repaired afterwards; it was the appointed road, and glory lay at its end. What was appointed for the Head is appointed for his body: through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22), and his path ends in glory.

Does destined for this apply to all suffering, or only persecution? Paul’s immediate subject is suffering for the gospel, the pressure that comes because you belong to Christ. But the principle reaches further: nothing comes to God’s children by accident, whether illness, loss or disappointment, and he works all of it for their good (Romans 8:28). That does not make every hardship good in itself, nor does it mean you must not seek relief. Pray for healing, seek justice, take the medicine. But you can do so knowing that you are where your Father has placed you, and that he has not lost track of you.

Is it wrong to try to avoid persecution? Not in itself. Jesus told his disciples to flee from one town to the next (Matthew 10:23), and Paul left Thessalonica and Damascus by night. What is wrong is avoiding it by denying Christ or compromising obedience. You may leave, keep a low profile in some settings, or use the law’s protection, as Paul used his citizenship. You may not lie about him, worship what he forbids, or abandon his people to save yourself.

On a Tuesday. Watch for where you are being nudged away from Christ: the joke you laugh along with, the habit quietly resumed, the conviction you no longer mention. Name it before God, who forgives it and does not let go of you, and stand where he has placed you.

verseByVerse.quote: For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction, just as it has come to pass, and just as you know. For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith, for fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you and our labor would be in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We kept telling you beforehand. With only a few weeks, Paul kept telling them: this will cost you. He did not win them with an easier offer and explain the terms later. Honest evangelism counts the cost (Luke 14:28).

Just as it has come to pass. A church told the truth in advance meets hardship saying, he said this would happen; a church promised an easy road meets the same hardship asking whether the whole thing was false.

I sent. Now the plural becomes singular. Paul admits his own fear, and he is not embarrassed by it.

The tempter. The tempter is the title used of Satan in the wilderness (Matthew 4:3), where the tactic was not violence but suggestion. Having cut the road (2:18), his strategy is to block the teacher, then work on the church, using suffering to tempt believers to give up.

The tempter has met his match. Paul feared the tempter because he knew his methods, and he knew who had beaten him. In the wilderness the Lord Jesus faced the same voice, hungry and alone, and answered every suggestion with the word of God (Matthew 4:1–11). Because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18). The church faced a defeated enemy, with a Saviour who knew his voice from the inside.

In vain. In vain is kenos, the empty word of 2:1, and here is the honest underside of that confidence. The apostle who writes so certainly about election in chapter 1 also lay awake fearing his work had come to nothing, and neither cancels the other. Strong faith does not mean the absence of anxiety.

What it does not mean. It does not mean true believers can be lost. Paul feared that their faith might prove false, which would show his labour fruitless. Timothy’s report proved it genuine.

If true believers cannot be lost, why did Paul fear? Because he could not see their hearts, only their outward profession, and he knew that some who make a start fall away because their faith was never real (Matthew 13:20–21; 1 John 2:19). God’s elect will persevere (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6), and they persevere by means: warnings, teaching, encouragement, prayer. Paul’s fear moved him to supply those means. So we hold both: unshakeable confidence in God’s keeping, and earnest care that no one drifts. The doctrine of perseverance is not a reason to stop watching over one another. And if you fear that the falling away describes you, the fear is itself a hopeful sign: those whose faith was never real seldom lie awake over it. Bring the fear to Christ, who keeps all who come to him (John 6:37).

How do I tell people the cost without frightening them away? Tell them the truth with the reward in view. Jesus never hid the cost of discipleship, and he never mentioned it without the treasure: whoever loses his life for my sake will find it (Matthew 16:25). Say plainly that following Christ may cost friendships, comfort and reputation. Then say why it is worth it: forgiveness, adoption, a living hope, Christ himself. People who are told the truth are not easily shaken when the trouble comes.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:6–13 – The News From Home, and a Prayer for Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Timothy’s good news is like new life to Paul. He prays to see them again and supply what their faith still lacks, and asks God to make their love overflow and their hearts blameless at the coming of the Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two persons, one verb

In verse 11 Paul names the Father and the Lord Jesus as two subjects and gives them one singular verb: the highest view of Christ, already present in the ordinary shape of a man’s prayers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What was lacking in their faith (v. 10) was not sincerity but completeness: the teaching Paul never got to give.

Now: Paul prays that a persecuted church would overflow in love not only for one another but “for all” (v. 12), the very population making its life hard.

verseByVerse.quote: But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us the good news of your faith and love and reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you— for this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now that Timothy has come. The letter changes temperature. Timothy had rejoined Paul in Corinth (Acts 18:5), and this letter was written in the first glow of his report.

Good news. Timothy, Paul says, gospelled us (euangelizomai), the only place in his letters where he uses the verb of anything but the gospel of Christ. News that a church was standing was, to him, good news of God’s work.

Three answers to three fears. Their faith: they had not been coaxed away. Their love: they had not turned on each other. And they remembered him kindly: the slanders had not worked.

Comforted about you. The apostle is comforted by the young converts. He was in Corinth by now, in weakness and fear and much trembling (1 Corinthians 2:3), and the Lord had to tell him in a vision not to be afraid (Acts 18:9–10).

The traffic runs both ways. In a healthy church the strengtheners are themselves held up by the perseverance of ordinary believers they worry about. If you have ever wondered whether your quiet faithfulness matters to anyone, this verse answers: it was what got Paul through Corinth.

Comfort that flows through Christ. Paul writes elsewhere: as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too (2 Corinthians 1:5). Their faith was Christ’s gift, and so was the comfort, carried down the road by a young man’s feet. Christ comforts his servants by keeping his people.

Is it all right to care what people think of me? It is right to care about being loved by your brothers and sisters, and to be grieved when relationships are damaged by slander. Paul did. What is wrong is letting their opinion govern your obedience (2:4). Paul would have preached the same gospel whether they thought well of him or not, but he was glad, deeply, that they did. Love wants to be loved back, and that is not vanity.

On a Tuesday. Send a word this week to a pastor, parent or mentor who has worried about you. When you hear good news of someone’s faith, pass it on; it may be the best thing a weary servant hears all month.

For worship. How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news (Isaiah 52:7). God sent such feet to a frightened apostle in Corinth: a young man coming down the road with word that a church was still standing. Every report of a believer still standing is a small echo of the prophet’s great news, that our God reigns and has bared his holy arm to save (Isaiah 52:7–10), accomplished in his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now we live. Paul does not say he is relieved; he says he is alive. The months of not knowing had been a kind of death, and Timothy’s news brought him back.

Love makes you a hostage. This is not the unhealthy dependence of a leader whose identity rests on his people’s performance; Paul has insisted he sought no glory from them. It is love, and love always makes your wellbeing hostage to someone else’s. That is not a defect in love; it is what love is.

Standing fast. The word is stēkō, to stand firm, a word that suits a soldier holding his position in the line. Paul uses it repeatedly of churches under pressure (Philippians 1:27; 4:1). It means you were still there when the pushing stopped.

In the Lord. Not by willpower or loyalty to Paul. The place they were holding was a person, and their strength was his. He had said of his sheep that no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28), and a church standing fast in the Lord is a church being held by him. The if is also a gentle encouragement: keep standing.

What does standing firm look like when I feel weak? It looks like still being there. Standing fast is not feeling strong; it is not leaving your post. It means you keep praying when prayer is dry, keep gathering with God’s people when you would rather stay home, keep refusing the sin that keeps coming back, and keep trusting Christ when you do not understand what he is doing. Because you stand in the Lord, your weakness does not decide the outcome. He holds the line with you.

verseByVerse.quote: For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you, for all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God, as we pray most earnestly night and day that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you? It is a real question, not a rhetorical flourish, and Paul does not answer it. He has run out of ways to say thank you. The joy is larger than the vocabulary available for it. And the thanks goes to God, since he is the one who kept them.

Before our God. Joy brought into God’s presence, because he did it.

Most earnestly night and day. The word (hyperekperissou) is a piled-up compound: beyond, beyond measure. And night and day is the phrase he used in 2:9 of working at his trade.

And supply what is lacking in your faith? This phrase needs care, because it can sound like a rebuke, and it is not one. Paul has just spent eight verses celebrating their faith. The word is katartizō, to put a thing into working order: it is used of the disciples mending their nets (Matthew 4:21), of a doctor setting a bone, and of God equipping his people for every good work (Hebrews 13:21). What is lacking is not sincerity but completeness: the teaching he never had time to give in a stay of a few weeks. Chapters 4 and 5 begin to supply it, on holiness, love, and the return of Christ.

Already full in Christ. What could be lacking in their faith? Not Christ. Paul tells another young church that in Christ the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him (Colossians 2:9–10). What was missing would be supplied not by adding a technique, experience or teacher alongside Christ, but by knowing more of the Christ they already had. Growth in faith is always growth into Christ, never away from him to something more.

How do I know what is lacking in my faith? There is a deficiency that is a fault, and there is a deficiency that is simply an unfinished education: gaps where nobody ever taught you. Paul’s response to the second is not reproach. It is to want to come and fill them in. So ask honestly: where do I not know what the Bible teaches? Where do I believe but not obey? Where does fear still rule? Then seek the remedy God provides: sit under faithful preaching, read whole books of Scripture, ask a mature believer to help you, and pray for growth. Gaps are expected; staying content with them is not.

Is my faith real if it has gaps? Yes. Every believer’s faith is incomplete in this life. The Thessalonians had a famous faith (1:8) that still lacked things. Real faith is not perfect faith; it is faith that rests on Christ and wants to grow. The fact that you notice gaps and want them filled is itself a sign of life.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father and the Lord Jesus. Two subjects, the Father and the Lord Jesus, and in the Greek the verb is singular. Paul names two persons acting as one, without explanation; a prayer addressed to the Father and the Son together assumes that the Son is God, and it shows how early and how instinctively the highest view of Christ was in place.

In the flow. Verses 11 to 13 close the first half of the letter and open the second. Paul asks for three things: a clear road back to them (v. 11), love that overflows (v. 12), and hearts made holy for Christ’s coming (v. 13). Chapters 4 and 5 then take up those very themes: holiness (4:1–8), love (4:9–12) and the coming of the Lord (4:13–5:11). Paul prays first for what he is about to teach.

Direct our way to you. The verb (kateuthynō) means to make straight, to clear a road, the opposite of Satan cutting into it (2:18). The enemy obstructs, the Sovereign governs, and only one is being prayed to.

What Paul does with frustration. He does not rebuke the devil; he asks God to clear the road, and gets on with the work he can do from where he is.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Father and the Son are one person. They are distinct persons who act as one God.

Is it right to pray to Jesus, or only to the Father? Both are right. The usual pattern of Christian prayer is to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18). But Scripture also shows believers praying to Jesus directly: Stephen called on him as he died (Acts 7:59), Paul pleaded with the Lord about his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:8), and here he prays to the Father and the Son together. Because the Son is God, he may be addressed in prayer and worshipped. You will not offend the Father by speaking to his Son.

What should I make of it when God does not answer my prayer the way I asked? Keep praying, and keep watching for what he does instead. Paul did not get his visit for years, but God answered the deeper request: the church was strengthened and Paul’s love reached them, through a letter. God always hears his children, and he gives what we would ask for if we knew what he knows. A no or a not yet from a wise Father is still an answer, and often a better one.

For worship. The Father and the Son act as one, and they rule every road on earth. No enemy can close what they open. The same Lord Jesus who is addressed in this prayer is the way to the Father, and he has made the road to God straight for us by his blood. Every road his people travel, blocked or open, runs at last to his Father’s house.

verseByVerse.quote: and may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, as we do for you, so that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Increase and abound in love. The second petition asks for love, and the verbs are extravagant. The first (pleonazō) means to multiply; the second (perisseuō) to overflow, like a river over its banks. He is asking for a flood.

For one another and for all. The second phrase is the sharp one. A community under hostility naturally turns inward, the beginning of a sect. Paul prays that a persecuted church would overflow with love toward the very population making its life difficult, including its persecutors (Matthew 5:44).

As we do for you. Paul’s own affection, shown for two chapters, is the measure.

Who produces it. May the Lord make you increase: Paul asks God to do it in them rather than telling them to try harder. The commands come in chapter 4, but the order is the order everywhere in his letters: ask God for what you then go and work at.

Blameless in holiness. Establish is the buttressing word of verse 2 (stērizō): what Timothy was sent to do, Paul now asks God to do. Blameless means without just accusation, and holiness is being set apart for God and made like him. No small request, for the God before whom they will stand is the one the seraphim call holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:3), and before whom even Isaiah cried that he was undone.

Before our God and Father. At the judgement, with nothing that can be justly charged against us.

With all his saints. Christ’s return, the parousia again. His saints, his holy ones, may be the angels who accompany him (Matthew 25:31), on the pattern of Zechariah 14:5, where the LORD comes and all the holy ones with him; or believers who have died, whom God will bring with him (4:14); or both. Paul has borrowed a prophet’s picture of the LORD arriving in judgement and applied it, without comment, to Jesus.

Where Christians differ: coming for his saints, or with them? Some dispensationalists (Christians who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras and expect separate futures for Israel and the church) distinguish Christ coming for his saints (a secret rapture) from coming with his saints (seven years later). They hold it out of a careful reading of prophecy and a real longing for Christ’s appearing, and this commentary honours them as brothers. This commentary’s view: Paul describes one coming, at which Christ brings the souls of departed believers with him, raises their bodies, gathers the living, and judges the world (4:14–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). He comes both for and with his saints in a single, visible, glorious return. There is no secret rapture. Paul’s second letter adds that this one coming will be preceded by the rebellion and the revealing of the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:1–3): it is near and certain, but it will not come unheralded.

How can anyone be blameless before God? In two ways, both by grace. First, believers are already counted righteous in Christ: his perfect obedience and his death are credited to them, so that no charge can stand (Romans 8:33–34). Second, God is making them holy in fact, a work he begins at conversion and completes at Christ’s coming, when we shall be like him (1 John 3:2). Theologians call the first justification, God declaring the guilty righteous for Christ’s sake, and the second sanctification, God making them holy over a lifetime. Paul prays for the second on the basis of the first. You will stand blameless on that day not because you finally got it right, but because Christ did, and because the God who began the work will finish it (5:23–24).

How do I love people who make my life difficult? Start by asking God for it, as Paul does; it is his gift before it is your effort. Then do concrete good: pray for them specifically, speak well of them where you honestly can, refuse revenge, and look for a practical kindness. Love is not pretending the harm did not happen, and it does not require you to stay in danger or to trust someone who has not changed. But it does wish them good, and it leaves judgement to God.
