5.title: Children of the Day
5.overview: After answering what happens to believers who die, Paul answers the next question, “When?”, by declining to give a date. The day of the Lord will come like a thief on a world saying “peace and security”, but it will not catch the children of the day unprepared, because God has appointed them to salvation through Jesus, who died for them. After instructions for church life the letter ends with a prayer that the God of peace will make them wholly holy, and a promise: “He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The day of the Lord will come unexpectedly, and ruin will fall on those who feel secure. But believers belong to the day, so they stay awake and sober, armed with faith, love and hope.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not destined for wrath

God’s purpose for his people was settled in advance, and settled on salvation rather than wrath (v. 9), not because of their performance but because the Lord Jesus “died for us” (v. 10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Peace and security” was close to an imperial slogan, and Paul names it as the moment of collapse.

Now: Paul tells them what they are, children of the day, before he tells them to stay awake (vv. 5–6). Getting that order backwards produces exhausted Christians.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need to have anything written to you. For you yourselves are fully aware that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Thessalonians 5 turns from comfort about the dead to readiness for the living: the day of the Lord will come like a thief, but believers are children of the day (vv. 1–11); then life in the church (vv. 12–22); and a closing prayer and promise that the faithful God will sanctify them completely for Christ’s coming (vv. 23–28).

Times and seasons. Chapter 4 answered the question they had asked: what about our dead? Chapter 5 answers the next one: when? Paul’s answer is a polite refusal. The two words, chronos and kairos, together mean simply when.

Echoing his Lord. He is echoing Jesus: it is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority (Acts 1:7), the same pair of words. Paul had taught them not a schedule but a certainty and a posture.

The day has a face. The day of the LORD comes from the prophets: the day God settles accounts, darkness and not light for people who assumed it would be good news for them (Amos 5:18–20; Joel 2:31). Paul hands that name to Jesus without a word of explanation, and so the day now has a face. The Lord who is coming is the Jesus they already know, who came once, openly, to die for them (v. 10), and will come again to gather the people he died for. That is why Paul can leave the date unknown and the church unafraid. For the secure world the day is ruin; for those in Christ it is the arrival of their Saviour, because the darkness the prophets warned of has already fallen once, on him.

Like a thief. The image comes from Jesus himself (Matthew 24:43; Revelation 16:15). A thief is dangerous not because he is malicious but because he does not send word, which is why calculating the date is not merely difficult but a contradiction of the teaching.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the day will be secret. It will be sudden, but visible to all.

Then why do so many people try to work out the date? Because uncertainty is uncomfortable, and a date feels like control. But every attempt has failed, and some have done real harm: believers who sold homes, quit jobs or lost faith when the date passed. Jesus said that even the angels do not know (Matthew 24:36). The right response to not knowing when is to be ready always. If someone tells you they have found the date, or that it must be within a certain number of years, you can kindly set it aside. The Lord has told us everything we need, and he has not told us that.

After nearly two thousand years, was the early church simply wrong? A sceptic often says so, but look at what Paul actually taught: not a date, but that no date can be known. No New Testament writer sets a date for Christ’s return. The hardest sayings are those such as this generation will not pass away until all these things take place (Matthew 24:34); many careful readers take them of the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, which did come within that generation, and believers hold Scripture true while admitting that such texts need care. It says the last days began when he came (Hebrews 1:2), so that his return is the next great act in God’s plan, and that is what near means. And Scripture itself answers the delay. With the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and he is not slow but patient, not wishing that any should perish but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:8–9). Every year he waits is another year of mercy to a world that does not deserve it.

Should the signs in the news make me think the end is very near? The end may be near; it has been near, in the biblical sense, since the ascension (Romans 13:11–12; James 5:8). Wars, earthquakes and troubles are, Jesus said, the beginning of the birth pains, not the end itself (Matthew 24:6–8), and they have marked every age. Read the news as a reminder that this world is passing, not as a code to crack. Paul’s second letter adds that certain events, the rebellion and the revealing of the man of lawlessness, come first (2 Thessalonians 2:3), so no one should be stampeded by date-setters. Live each day ready to meet him, and plan your life as though he might not come for a hundred years. Both are faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: While people are saying, "There is peace and security," then sudden destruction will come upon them as labor pains come upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peace and security. Those two words together, eirēnē kai asphaleia, were probably close to a Roman slogan. The pax Romana was the empire’s proudest claim and its central promise: peace, and safety, guaranteed by the legions, and coins and inscriptions celebrated both. Thessalonica, a free city that had backed the winning side in Rome’s civil wars and prospered for it, had every reason to believe the advertising. So had Jerusalem when its false prophets said peace, peace, when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14). Paul seems to echo the slogan at the very moment of collapse: a civilisation announcing its own permanence is the least prepared thing there is.

Another king, Jesus. The mob that dragged Jason before the city rulers charged the believers with saying that there is another king, Jesus (Acts 17:7). Rome offered peace won by the sword. Christ made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), when he took on himself the ruin this verse describes, and his is the only peace and security that will still be standing on the day of the Lord.

Sudden destruction. The word is olethros, ruin: not annihilation, but eternal loss, the shutting out from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9).

As labour pains. Labour is sudden in its onset, but not unexpected: the woman has known for months that it is coming. The day is unpredictable in timing and entirely predictable in fact.

They will not escape. The negative is emphatic: they will by no means get clear.

A future the slogan never had. Labour ends in a birth, and the New Testament uses birth-pain language for the end of the age because the pains precede a new creation (Romans 8:22). Paul does not develop it here, but the picture carries a future the slogan never had.

Is this destruction really eternal? Is hell real? Yes. The destruction of the day of the Lord is not a temporary trouble but final ruin, described elsewhere as eternal destruction away from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9) and as conscious, unending punishment (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11). It is the most sobering truth in Scripture, and Jesus spoke of it more than anyone. It is not taught to frighten Christians, who are not destined for wrath (v. 9), but to wake the sleeping while there is time, and to show us what Christ saved us from.

Where do I find false security in my own life? Wherever you feel safe without God: in savings, health, a career, a good reputation, a country’s stability, or even a past religious experience you no longer live by. None of these is wrong to have; all are wrong to rest on. Ask what you would still have if each were removed tomorrow. The only security that survives the day of the Lord is being in Christ.
verseByVerse.note: “Peace and security” may echo the boasts of the Roman order.

parallels.desc: Peace, peace, when there is no peace

verseByVerse.quote: But you are not in darkness, brothers, for that day to surprise you like a thief. For you are all children of light, children of the day. We are not of the night or of the darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not in darkness. But you: the paragraph turns from the people saying peace and security to the church. Paul does not say they will avoid the day, but that it will not surprise them.

To surprise you like a thief. The thief is a problem for the household that is asleep, not for a house with its lights on. Believers do not know the date, but they will not be caught unprepared.

Children of light. Then the identity, and it comes before any command. The Hebrew idiom son of means belonging to, characterised by: sons of light are people whose nature is light (Ephesians 5:8). That means God has given them a new heart. Where once they loved the dark and hid from God, they now love what is true and want their deeds to be seen as done in God (John 3:19–21). Paul is not telling them to become something; he is telling them what they are. And the little word all matters: not only the mature or the leaders, but every believer, including the fainthearted and the weak of verse 14.

Believe in the light. The phrase comes from Jesus: while you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light (John 12:36; 8:12). The light these believers belong to is not a moral climate but a Person, and they became his by believing in him. That is why Paul slips at once from you to we.

Identity before command. He does not say: stay awake, and then you will be children of light. He says: you are children of light, therefore stay awake.

How did I become a child of light? By God’s act, not yours. God, who said let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). He delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13). You did not climb into the light; the light came to you. That is why the word all can stand: every believer is there by the same grace.

I still do things that belong to the darkness. Am I really a child of light? If you trust Christ, yes. Children of light still sin, but they no longer belong to the night, and they cannot be at home there. The sign is not sinlessness but what you do with sin: you hate it, bring it into the light by confessing it, and turn from it (1 John 1:7–9). Live like what you are. When you stumble in the dark, remember whose child you are and walk back toward the light.

For worship. God is light, and in him is no darkness at all. Yet at noon on the day he died, darkness came over all the land, and he was forsaken in it, so that children of the night could be called children of the day. Glory to the Son, who entered our night so that we could belong to his morning.

verseByVerse.quote: So then let us not sleep, as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, are drunk at night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us not sleep. The sleep here is not the tender word for the Christian dead of 4:13–15 but spiritual carelessness. And it is let us: Paul does not consider himself immune.

Keep awake and be sober. Keep awake (grēgoreō): the word for the watchman, and for the disciples in Gethsemane, who failed at it. Be sober (nēphō): clear-headed, in possession of your judgement, able to see what is actually there.

Watching for the master of the house. Keep awake is Jesus’ own word: the doorkeeper stays awake because no one knows whether the master will come in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow or in the morning (Mark 13:33–37). Christian wakefulness is not nervous vigilance. It is a servant listening for a footstep he loves (John 14:3).

The underrated virtue. Sobriety is not solemnity: this letter commands rejoicing ten verses later. It is the capacity to know what is temporary and what is permanent, and not to be talked into a false estimate of either.

At night. In the ancient city the night belonged to sleeping and carousing (Romans 13:12–13). These people do not belong to the night at all, so moral drowsiness in a Christian is out of place, like a man asleep in the street at noon. Paul is not threatening them; he is pointing out that they are dressed for the wrong hour.

What does spiritual sleep look like in an ordinary Christian? It rarely looks like rebellion. It looks like drift: prayer becoming occasional, the Bible unopened for weeks, church attended without attention, sins no longer noticed, eternity no longer thought about, the heart filled with screens and schedules until God is crowded out. The sleeper does not feel asleep. That is why Paul says let us: we need one another to notice and to wake each other up.

Does be sober forbid alcohol? Scripture does not forbid alcohol itself; wine is a gift that gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15), and Jesus made it. It does forbid drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18), and here it uses drunkenness as a picture of a dulled mind. Some Christians choose to abstain, for their own sake or for others, and that is a wise freedom. Whatever you drink, never let anything, alcohol, entertainment, busyness or anxiety, cloud your judgement about what matters most.

verseByVerse.quote: But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we belong to the day. Sobriety is not achieved by trying harder to concentrate. It is achieved by getting dressed.

The breastplate of faith and love. The picture is a soldier on night watch, drawn from Isaiah, where the LORD puts on righteousness as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation (Isaiah 59:17), and the armour is the triad of the letter’s first paragraph (1:3).

The armour the Redeemer wore. In Isaiah the LORD arms himself because he sees no one to intervene, and the passage ends with the promise that a Redeemer will come to Zion (Isaiah 59:16–20; Romans 11:26). The armour was first worn by the one who came to save, alone, and he now gives it to those he rescued. Believers are clothed in the gear of a victory already won.

The helmet. Faith and love cover the chest; hope is the helmet: it keeps you thinking straight. A church losing its grip on the future becomes unable to think clearly about the present, which is what had happened when their friends died. And the armour is entirely defensive: Paul is equipping them to stay upright until the day comes.

What does it mean to put on faith, love and hope in practice? It means deliberately taking hold of them each day, as a soldier straps on armour before the watch. Put on faith by reminding yourself of God’s promises and trusting them in the decisions in front of you. Put on love by deciding, before you meet people, to seek their good. Put on hope by setting your mind on Christ’s return and your inheritance, especially when discouragement starts to talk. You do this through Scripture, prayer and the fellowship of the church, which is where the armour is kept.

Is the hope of salvation certain, or might I lose it? Certain, because it rests on God’s appointment, as the next verse says: God has not destined us for wrath but to obtain salvation. Biblical hope is not maybe; it is a sure thing not yet seen (Romans 8:24–25). It is called a helmet precisely because it holds when you are struck. If you are in Christ, your future salvation is as secure as his resurrection.

For worship. The Lord who arms his people went into his own battle stripped. For our helmet he wore thorns; for our breastplate his side was opened by a spear. He took the blows unguarded so that faith, love and hope could cover us through the night.

parallels.desc: righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation

verseByVerse.quote: For God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not destined for wrath. Here is the ground under everything, answering the fear the wrath language has raised since 1:10. The verb (tithēmi) means to appoint: God’s purpose settled in advance, and settled not on wrath, and the reason is not their performance.

To obtain salvation. This is election again (1:4; 2 Thessalonians 2:13). To obtain is a word for coming into possession, as an heir comes into an estate: they are not hoping to be spared; they are on their way to collect.

Who died for us. There is the mechanism, the only place in this letter where Paul states the substitution directly. For us (hyper hēmōn) means on our behalf and in our place. They are not destined for wrath, not because God overlooks things, but because someone else stood where they were standing and bore the wrath himself (Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:2): his death turned away God’s just anger, so that for those in him there is none left to fall.

Awake or asleep. The clause ties the two chapters together: awake meaning alive, asleep meaning dead, at Christ’s return (4:13–18). Alive or dead when he comes, the outcome is identical. Paul does not promise they will be alive at the coming, and in fact every one of them died; the promise is that it will not matter.

Does this mean the church will be taken away before the tribulation? Pretribulational Christians argue so, out of a real concern to honour God’s promise: the church is not destined for wrath, so it cannot go through the tribulation. But wrath here is God’s final judgement, from which Jesus delivers us (1:10; Romans 5:9), not the trouble Christians may suffer in this world, which Paul says they are destined for (3:3). Believers are kept from God’s wrath, not from every tribulation.

Where Christians differ: not destined for wrath. Some use this verse to argue that believers will be raptured before a future tribulation. This commentary’s view: The wrath here is God’s final judgement on the ungodly, from which Christ’s death saves believers (1:10; Romans 5:9). It does not promise exemption from suffering or persecution before the end; the Thessalonians were already suffering (3:3). Believers will be delivered from God’s wrath, not from all tribulation (John 16:33; Acts 14:22).

Why did Christ have to die for us? Could God not simply forgive? God’s forgiveness is free to us but not cheap. Sin is a real offence against a holy God, and a just judge cannot simply ignore it (Exodus 34:7; Romans 3:25–26). The wonder of the gospel is that God himself, in the person of his Son, took the penalty, so that he could be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. Christ died for us: in our place, under our condemnation, so that the wrath we deserved is spent and gone. That is why God can say to believers, with perfect justice, you are not destined for wrath.

How do I know I am destined for salvation and not wrath? Not by peering into God’s decrees but by looking to Christ. Do you trust him who died for us? Then this verse is about you. Those whom God appointed to salvation, he calls to faith (Romans 8:30), and faith is the sign of the appointment. If you are afraid, do not look first at your feelings or your record; look at the cross, where the wrath fell on him, and rest there.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Encourage one another. The second time in two paragraphs Paul has ended a passage about the last day with an instruction to talk to each other (4:18). Teaching about the end is given to be used on people who need it.

What they are to say. The encouragement Paul means is not general cheerfulness but the sentence he has just written: Christ died for us so that, awake or asleep, we will live with him. One believer reminding another of that is laying Christ again as the foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11).

Build one another up. The word is oikodomeō, constructing a building, behind our word edify. Encouragement is structural work on another person, and it is one another: ordinary members, not only the leaders of verse 12.

Just as you are doing. Once more the gracious ending (4:1, 10): Paul names what is already true and asks for more of it, which is harder than criticism, and a good deal more effective.

How do I build someone up if I am not a teacher? With ordinary words, aimed well. Tell someone specifically where you see God’s grace in them. Share a verse that helped you this week. Remind a discouraged friend of a promise. Ask how you can pray, and then do it, and tell them you did. Thank someone for serving. Speak hope about Christ’s return to someone who is weary. Building up is usually a sentence at a time, given at the right moment, and anyone who loves Christ and his people can do it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to life together: honour those who lead, care for each struggling member in the way he needs, never repay evil, rejoice, pray and give thanks, and test everything.
verseByVerse.theology:
Discernment instead of either extreme

Verses 19–22 refuse both easy positions, contempt for what the Spirit gives and credulity, and ask for testing: holding fast what is good and abstaining from what is bad.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A congregation only months old already had leaders, honoured “because of their work” (v. 13).

Now: Verse 14 asks every member, not only leaders, to read the person in front of them before deciding whether to warn, encourage or hold up.

verseByVerse.quote: We ask you, brothers, to respect those who labor among you and are over you in the Lord and admonish you, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who labour among you. Three descriptions of the same people, one job seen from three sides: church leaders, probably the elders, though the word is not used. They labour (kopiaō, work to the point of weariness, 1:3); they are over you (proistēmi, to lead, and also to care for); and they admonish (noutheteō, correction meant to change someone).

How young this was. This church was months old, and it already had recognised leaders, described not by title but by their work. The first thing owed them is respect, literally to know them: noticing who is doing the work.

Esteem them very highly. Paul stacks the intensifiers again (hyperekperissou, beyond all measure, 3:10). But the ground is stated exactly: not their office, gifts or personality, but their work. And in love, not merely as duty: a congregation that grasps what the work costs, the broken nights, the conversation nobody wants to have, will find the esteem easier to give.

Over you in the Lord. Their leadership is in the Lord: exercised inside Christ’s rule and answerable to him, not lords over the flock (1 Peter 5:3). They serve the one who came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:44–45). A church that honours its faithful leaders is honouring Christ’s gift, and a leader who domineers has forgotten whose flock it is.

Be at peace among yourselves. Having told them to esteem certain people very highly, Paul probably guards it: not so highly that you form parties around them. Peace among the members is the condition in which anyone can lead at all.

What if my church leaders get things wrong? They will, because they are sinners like you. Honour does not mean pretending they are perfect. Pray for them first. If something is a matter of preference, let it go graciously. If it is a real concern, go to them privately and humbly, as you would want to be approached (Matthew 18:15). If there is serious sin or false teaching, Scripture gives a careful process (1 Timothy 5:19–20). And abuse of any kind must never be covered up: it is to be brought into the light and, where it is a crime, reported, whoever the leader is. Respect for leaders never means silence about harm.

How do I actually show esteem to my pastor and elders? Pray for them by name, regularly. Tell them specifically when their ministry has helped you. Receive their teaching and admonition without resentment (Hebrews 13:17). Do not gossip about them or join in when others do. Support them practically, including generously providing for those who teach (1 Timothy 5:17–18; Galatians 6:6). Care for their families. Turn up and serve. A leader who knows he is loved can bear far more of the work.

verseByVerse.quote: And we urge you, brothers, admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we urge you, brothers. Now Paul turns to what members owe each other, all the brothers, not just leaders, and three different people get three different treatments.

Admonish the idle. The word ataktoi first described soldiers out of rank, and in everyday use often meant the idle: the problem of 4:11 (2 Thessalonians 3:6–12). What they need is not sympathy. They need to be told.

Encourage the fainthearted. Oligopsychoi, literally small-souled: the person whose courage has run low. In a church burying friends there would have been plenty. Tell a frightened person to pull himself together and you have made him worse. Comfort them.

Help the weak. The verb (antechomai) means to hold on to, to support, like taking someone’s arm. The weak, in faith, conscience, body or circumstance, need not advice but someone bearing some of the weight.

Three troubles, three cures. Giving the wrong response does damage. The lazy man comforted stays lazy; the frightened man rebuked despairs; the weak man exhorted simply falls over. Wise care diagnoses before it treats.

Each one as the Lord treated them. Paul is not inventing a technique. He is describing how the Lord Jesus dealt with people. He warned the careless plainly, as in the parable of the servant who buried his master’s money and blamed his fear (Matthew 25:24–27). To terrified men in a boat at night he said, Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid (Matthew 14:27). And when Peter began to sink, Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him (Matthew 14:31), the very gesture that the word help describes. A church that warns, encourages and holds up the weak is doing to one another what its Lord has been doing to each of them.

Be patient with them all. Makrothymeō: long-tempered, slow to boil. All three will try you: the idle will not start, the fainthearted will not be reassured, the weak will need holding up again next week. Patience, which the Spirit grows in us (Galatians 5:22), keeps you doing the right thing for the eleventh time.

How do I know which one a person needs? Listen before you speak, and ask questions. Is the problem that they will not, or that they cannot, or that they are afraid? The idle person usually knows what to do and is not doing it; the fainthearted person wants to but is crushed by fear; the weak person is willing but lacks strength. Many people are a mixture, and the same person can need different things in different seasons. Pray for wisdom (James 1:5), take time to know people, and be willing to change your approach when you see you have misjudged.

What if I am the fainthearted or the weak one? Then this verse is God’s instruction to your church to care for you, and there is no shame in receiving it. Tell someone honestly how you are. Let others hold your arm. You do not have to pretend to be strong in order to belong. The Lord does not break a bruised reed or quench a smouldering wick (Isaiah 42:3), and he has told his people to treat you the same way.

For worship. Before we were ever told to be patient with them all, he was patient with us: with the idle, the fainthearted who ran, the weak who could not keep awake one hour. In Paul, the foremost of sinners, Christ Jesus displayed his perfect patience (1 Timothy 1:16), and every slow-tempered word we give a struggling brother is drawn from that supply.
verseByVerse.note: “Idle” may mean those who had stopped working, perhaps expecting the Lord’s imminent return.

verseByVerse.quote: See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always seek to do good to one another and to everyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See that no one repays. Not merely do not repay evil, but see to it that no one does: retaliation is made a community problem (Romans 12:17; 1 Peter 3:9). These were people driven from families and squeezed out of trades, with genuine grievances against identifiable neighbours. This is not an ethic offered to the comfortable.

Always seek to do good. The verb (diōkō) means to chase after, the same word used for persecuting. They were being pursued with evil; they were to pursue with good, believers and everyone else.

The persecutor who was pursued. Paul had stood on the receiving end of love your enemies (Luke 6:27–28). He had once pursued the church, the same verb, and the risen Christ met him asking, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). The Lord chased his enemy down with mercy and made him an apostle.

What makes it possible. Two things in this letter make this hard command possible. The Lord is an avenger (4:6), so the wronged Christian is not required to secure justice himself. And these people are not destined for wrath (5:9): they have received the treatment they are now asked to extend. Refusing revenge is not pretending the wrong did not happen. It is handing it to a court that will actually deal with it.

Does doing good to someone who hurt me mean I must trust them or stay near them? No. Doing good is not the same as giving access. You can refuse revenge, pray for someone and wish them well while keeping a safe distance, especially where there has been abuse or danger. Forgiveness releases the debt to God; trust is rebuilt only where there is real repentance and change, and sometimes not at all. Reporting a crime or seeking protection is not repaying evil for evil; it is seeking justice by the means God has given.

What does do good look like toward someone I resent? Small, concrete, real things. Speak of them fairly. Refuse to join in mockery. Pray for their blessing, and mean it as far as you can. Help them when they are in need. Answer a sharp word with a gentle one. You may not feel love at first, but deeds of good often lead the heart, and they always honour Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoice always. Two words in Greek. Paul is not asking a grieving, persecuted church to pretend. Joy here is what it was in 1:6: given by the Holy Spirit in the middle of much affliction, possible always because its ground is outside the circumstances (Philippians 4:4).

Pray without ceasing. The word (adialeiptōs) could describe a persistent cough: something that keeps recurring. Paul is describing a life in which the line to God is never actually closed: regular times of prayer, and between them a heart that keeps turning to him through the day.

Give thanks in all circumstances. In all circumstances, not for all circumstances. Paul does not ask anyone to be grateful for a death or a betrayal, but for thanksgiving to continue inside such things, because God’s goodness does not pause and he is at work in all of them (Romans 8:28).

The will of God in Christ Jesus. The second time the letter has told us plainly what God’s will is; the first was sanctification (4:3). The three are held together for a reason: joy without prayer becomes shallow optimism; prayer without thanksgiving becomes a list of complaints; thanksgiving without joy becomes a duty.

On the night he was betrayed. And all of it is in Christ Jesus. Paul knew of a thanksgiving offered in the darkest circumstances there have ever been: on the night when he was betrayed the Lord Jesus took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it (1 Corinthians 11:23–24). He gave thanks with the cross a few hours away, over bread that meant his own body given. This will of God is not an ideal we strain toward alone. It is the life of the Son, who rejoiced, prayed and gave thanks perfectly, now lived out by his Spirit in those joined to him. We never keep these three perfectly; he did, in our place, and for his sake our faltering prayers and thanks are accepted. Our thanks in hard places is an echo of his.

How can I rejoice when I am grieving or depressed? Christian joy is not the same as a happy mood, and it can coexist with tears and even with dark seasons of the mind. The psalms of lament are full of sorrow, and most of them still turn toward God and end with trust. Joy at its root is the settled fact that Christ is yours and you are his, and you can hold on to that even when you cannot feel it. If you are depressed, seek help from your doctor as well as your church; that is not a lack of faith. And let others rejoice on your behalf for a while, and pray for you, until joy returns.

How do I pray without ceasing in a busy life? Build habits that keep the line open. Keep regular times of prayer, morning and evening if you can. Then attach short prayers to ordinary moments: waking, meals, the commute, the start of a meeting, a hard email, a piece of good news. Turn worries into requests the moment they arise, and turn pleasures into thanks. Over time, turning to God becomes a reflex, like the persistent cough Paul’s word describes.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good. Abstain from every form of evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not quench the Spirit. Five short commands about the Spirit’s work in the assembly. The verb (sbennymi) is used of putting out a fire (Acts 2:3). You extinguish a fire by smothering it, or by simply not feeding it: by sin, by neglect, or by suppressing his work in the church.

Do not despise prophecies. Some in Thessalonica were apparently dismissive of prophetic speech. One can see why: the second letter deals with a claimed message saying the day of the Lord had already come (2 Thessalonians 2:2), and the instinct is to shut the whole thing down.

Test everything. Paul refuses that instinct. Not credulity; not cynicism; testing: dokimazō, the assayer’s word from 2:4 (1 John 4:1). Now that the apostolic word stands complete in Scripture, every claim to speak for God is tested against it.

What the Spirit always says. Testing is not guesswork, because the Spirit has one consistent subject: he will glorify me (John 16:14). So the New Testament’s tests turn on Christ (1 Corinthians 12:3; 1 John 4:2). A word that makes much of the speaker or the experience, and little of the crucified and risen Lord, has already failed.

Hold fast what is good. Testing has two results. Keep what passes the test: discernment that only ever rejects has failed at half its job. And whatever the testing shows to be bad, drop it entirely, whatever authority was claimed for it.

Every form, or all appearance? The KJV reads abstain from all appearance of evil, and it has often been taken to mean avoiding anything that might look wrong to others. The ESV’s every form of evil is the better rendering: Paul means to shun evil in every shape it takes, not to live by other people’s impressions. Avoiding needless offence is wise, but that is not the point of this verse.

Does this mean prophecy continues today? At Thessalonica, before the New Testament was written, prophets spoke words from the Spirit in the gathered church, and Paul tells the church to weigh them, not despise them. Continuationist Christians (those who believe all the gifts of the New Testament continue today) believe such prophecy continues, and many of them are wise and godly believers whose reasons deserve a hearing. The more likely reading is that prophecy as new revelation belonged with the apostles to the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20), and ceased when the Scriptures were complete. The principle stands: test everything; hold fast what is good. Every claim to speak for God must be tested by his written word.

Where Christians differ: prophecy today. Continuationists see here a command for churches to welcome prophecy today; some cessationists dismiss the passage. This commentary’s view: In the apostolic churches, before the New Testament was complete, prophecy was an active gift, and Paul commanded the church neither to despise nor accept it uncritically. With the completion of Scripture, revelatory prophecy has ceased (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 1:1–2). But the principles remain: do not quench the Spirit, who speaks through the word; test every teaching and claim by Scripture; hold to what is good. These apply to preaching, teaching and every claim of spiritual guidance today. This view is held with charity toward continuationist brothers and sisters.

Open, and awake. The five refuse both of the easy positions. A church can be so afraid of disorder that it quenches the Spirit, or so afraid of quenching the Spirit that it swallows anything. Paul asks for the harder combination: open, and awake.

How might a cessationist church quench the Spirit? By treating the Bible as a museum piece rather than the living voice of God; by preaching without prayer or dependence on the Spirit; by resisting conviction of sin; by stifling the gifts he does give, such as teaching, encouragement, mercy and service; or by a coldness that never expects God to change anyone. The Spirit speaks through the word, so the surest way to quench him is to stop listening to Scripture expectantly. Cessationism rightly guards the closed canon; it must never become an excuse for spiritual deadness.

What if someone tells me God gave them a word for me? Listen respectfully, then test it by Scripture. If it contradicts the Bible, reject it, however sincere the speaker. If it is simply a biblical truth applied, such as a reminder of God’s promises or a warning against a sin Scripture names, you may receive it as good counsel, but its authority comes from Scripture, not from the claim. Do not make major decisions on the basis of such words alone. Ask wise, mature believers and your pastors. God’s will for you is found in his written word and in wise, prayerful obedience to it.

verseByVerse.ref: 5:23–28 – Kept Blameless, and the Last Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul prays that the God of peace will make them holy through and through until the Lord Jesus comes, and promises that he will. He asks for prayer, greetings for all and the letter read to everyone, and ends with grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Whole persons, and who does the keeping

“Spirit and soul and body” (v. 23) is a way of saying the whole of you, and they are to be kept by the God who calls them and is faithful (v. 24).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The oath of verse 27 ensured the letter reached every believer, the illiterate included.

Now: The holy kiss for all the brothers (v. 26) quietly undoes rank: you cannot greet someone as family every week and go on regarding him as beneath you.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God of peace himself. The letter turns to prayer. The God of peace: the God who makes peace with sinners through the blood of his Son. Himself: Paul has told them to be holy, to work, to love, to stay awake; now he prays, because nobody produces this by effort. And it is complete: holoteleis, through and through, right to the finish.

In the flow. Verses 23–24 echo the prayer that closed chapter 3 (3:13): Paul has wrapped his commands in prayer, because what he has commanded only God can produce.

Kept blameless. Be kept (tēreō, guarded) is passive. They are not keeping themselves; someone is keeping them, and the difference is the difference between exhaustion and rest. Every chapter of this letter has ended with Christ’s coming, and this one does too.

Blameless before whom? How can anyone who knows his own heart be without blame when the Lord Jesus comes? Paul answers elsewhere: Christ has reconciled us in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present us holy and blameless and above reproach before him (Colossians 1:22). The one before whom we must stand is the one who made us fit to stand. His death gives the blamelessness that counts before God now, and his Spirit works it out in spirit, soul and body, until the day we see him and are made like him (1 John 3:2).

Three parts or two? The threefold phrase raises an old question: is a person made of three parts or two? Some have read it as trichotomy: spirit as the God-ward faculty, soul as the conscious self, body as the physical frame, three compartments. The historic Reformed reading, from Calvin on, is dichotomy: spirit and soul name the one immaterial dimension of human nature from two angles, not two separate parts. Scripture sets the words side by side in parallel (Luke 1:46–47), and the pattern is familiar from Deuteronomy 6:5, love the LORD with all your heart and soul and might, which nobody takes as an anatomy. It is a way of saying the whole of you.

Where Christians differ: spirit, soul and body. Some (trichotomists) take this to mean humans have three distinct parts: spirit, soul and body. Others (dichotomists) hold two: body and soul (or spirit). This commentary’s view: Scripture usually describes humans as body and soul, or body and spirit, using soul and spirit interchangeably (Matthew 10:28; 1 Corinthians 7:34; Ecclesiastes 12:7). Paul here stresses the whole person, every aspect, not giving a technical anatomy. The majority Reformed view is that humans are a unity of body and soul (Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 17; Westminster 4.2).

Where Christians differ: entire sanctification. Some in the Wesleyan tradition, a tradition rich in earnest pursuit of holiness, take this verse to teach that believers can be sanctified entirely in this life, free from sin. This commentary’s view: Paul prays for complete sanctification, and God will accomplish it, at the coming of Christ. In this life, believers grow in holiness but remain sinners (1 John 1:8). Sanctification is complete at glorification (Philippians 3:12), as the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach (Westminster 13.2; 1689 13.2).

He will surely do it. Then the prayer becomes a promise. The calling is present tense, as in 2:12: he goes on calling. The guarantee is not their staying power but his character: he does not begin what he will not finish (Philippians 1:6; 1 Corinthians 1:8–9).

If God will do it, why should I make any effort? Because God sanctifies us through our effort, not instead of it. Paul can say in one breath, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work (Philippians 2:12–13). His promise is not a reason to stop fighting sin but the reason the fight is not hopeless. You strive because he is at work, and you rest because the outcome depends on him. Effort without the promise leads to despair; the promise without effort is a misreading of it.

Does my body matter to God as much as my soul? Yes. Paul prays for body as well as spirit and soul to be kept blameless. God made the body, the Son took a body, the Spirit dwells in the body, and the body will be raised. So what you do with your body, sexual purity, honest work, care for health, rest, and the use of your eyes, hands and tongue, is part of your holiness. Christianity is not a religion that despises the physical. It sanctifies it.

On a Tuesday. When you feel discouraged at how slowly you are changing, read verse 24 aloud: he who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it. Then take the next small step of obedience in front of you, and leave the finishing to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, pray for us. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I put you under oath before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, pray for us. The apostle who has prayed for them night and day (3:10) asks them to pray for him. Mutual intercession is the life of the church.

A holy kiss. The kiss on the cheek was an ordinary greeting between family and close friends, and it became the family greeting of the early church (Romans 16:16). What is not ordinary is the range: all the brothers. In a room containing slaves and masters, Jews and Greeks, the householder and the day labourer, that instruction dismantles something. Holy sets it apart from the ordinary social kiss.

Must Christians greet one another with a kiss today? The command is for a warm, sincere greeting between brothers and sisters, in the form one’s culture uses. Where a kiss carries that meaning, it may still be used; elsewhere a handshake or an embrace obeys the command. What matters is that no one in the church is left ungreeted, and that the greeting is pure and genuine.

Read to all the brothers. The verb is strong: to adjure, to place someone under solemn obligation, most probably because of the word all. Letters were read aloud; many believers could not read. Paul wants nobody left out, not the slaves who might miss a meeting, not the fainthearted and the weak he has just named. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read all the holy brothers; the earliest lack holy, so most modern Bibles omit it.

Before the Lord. The oath is sworn by the Lord, which in this letter almost always means Jesus. They had received Paul’s preaching as the word of God (2:13), and whoever hears Christ’s messengers hears him (Luke 10:16). So the letter is to be read to the whole assembly, as the Scriptures were read in the synagogue (Colossians 4:16). To keep it from any of them would be to stand between the Shepherd and his sheep.

How should I pray for my pastor and for missionaries? Pray as Paul asked elsewhere: that the word of the Lord may speed ahead and be honoured, that they may be delivered from wicked people (2 Thessalonians 3:1–2), that doors would open for the gospel and they would speak it clearly (Colossians 4:3–4), and that they would be bold (Ephesians 6:19–20). Pray for their holiness, their marriages and children, their health and their joy. Ask them what they need prayer for, and then tell them you prayed.
verseByVerse.note: The holy kiss was the family greeting of the early church.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grace to close. The letter opened with grace (1:1) and closes with it. Inside the frame stand a young church under persecution, a congregation burying its dead, a man answering slander, and a list of hard commands. All of it sits inside grace.

Grace arriving, grace staying. The greeting was grace to you: grace arriving. Here it is grace be with you: grace staying, accompanying them into whatever came next. Paul could not come himself; what he can send is this.

What came next. What came next was not easy. They would go on being a small, pressured minority in a proud Roman city. Paul would write a second letter, probably within months, because the confusion about the Lord’s coming had got worse. The last word he gives them is the thing that would still be true through all of it.

Grace with a name. Grace has a name and a history: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9). When the letter ends with grace, it ends with him, and the blessing is that he goes with them into whatever comes.

What is grace, exactly? Grace is God’s free, undeserved favour toward sinners in Christ, and his power at work in them. It is favour: God treats us not as our sins deserve but as his Son deserves. And it is power: the same grace that forgives also changes, strengthens and keeps (2 Corinthians 12:9; Titus 2:11–12). It is the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ because he is its source and its channel: he bought it at the cross and gives it from the throne. Every command in this letter is obeyed by it, and every promise is kept by it.

For worship. The grace the Lord gave a frightened church in a proud city has not grown thin with use. It was poured out at the cross, carried the Thessalonians through persecution and grief, and will bring his people home on the day of his coming.
